paper.citation: Mitchell A, Holding C, Greig M. The Influence of Injury History on Countermovement Jump Performance and Movement Strategy in Professional Soccer Players: Implications for Profiling and Rehabilitation Foci. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2021;30(5):768-773.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study compared 10 professional outfield soccer players with a prior lower-limb injury that kept them out of team training for 3 months or more (currently fit) with 10 players who had never had such an injury. Players performed double- and single-leg countermovement jumps (CMJ) on force plates, and jump height, flight time:contraction time ratio and force-time variables were compared. Double-leg CMJ did not differ between groups, whereas single-leg CMJ performance and movement strategy were impaired in previously injured players, including in the uninjured limb.
paper.tldr: In professional soccer players with a previous lower-limb injury, double-leg jumps looked normal, but single-leg CMJ showed weaker performance and altered force strategy, so single-leg testing may be more useful for profiling and choosing rehabilitation focus.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional profiling during a competitive season at one English Championship club. Previously injured (n=10) and non-injured (n=10) outfield players completed 5 double-leg jumps and 5 single-leg jumps per limb on a force plate sampled at 1000 Hz. Jump height, flight time:contraction time ratio, and eccentric and concentric force-time variables were compared with general linear models, with single-leg data pooled across limbs (n=20 per group) and a secondary analysis by affected limb (n=10 per group); stepwise regression examined the ordering of force variables.
paper.findings: Double-leg CMJ jump height (P=.447) and flight time:contraction ratio (P=.623) did not differ by group. Single-leg jump height (P=.007, partial eta squared 0.176) and flight time:contraction ratio (P=.005, partial eta squared 0.188) were lower in previously injured players, and the affected limb showed lower concentric peak force and rate of force development than non-injured players. The nonaffected limb also produced lower single-leg performance than non-injured players, which the authors attribute to cross-contamination. In non-injured players, eccentric rate of force development and concentric peak force accounted for up to 89% of the variation in CMJ performance, whereas injured players' main predictors were concentric-phase variables.
paper.limitations: The sample is small (10 per group), comes from one club, and was limited by squad size. Injury type, location, mechanism and time since injury were not considered. Single-leg data pool both limbs from the same players, so limb observations are not independent. It is a single cross-sectional test session, so no causal or rehabilitation outcome conclusions can be drawn. Some regression values differ between the Results text and Table 3, so the exact predictor ordering should be read with caution.
paper.practicalImplications: Single-leg CMJ with force-time metrics may reveal deficits that double-leg CMJ hides, so it can be considered for player profiling batteries. For previously injured players, the authors suggest tracking movement strategy, particularly eccentric force development and rate of force development, not just jump height. These findings are hypothesis-generating in a small sample and should be confirmed before they drive individual decisions.
paper.athleteDev: Single-leg CMJ with force-time metrics may be more sensitive than double-leg CMJ for profiling players with a prior injury because it limits interlimb compensation. Monitoring eccentric and concentric force development and rate of force development, not jump height alone, may give a fuller picture of these players' neuromuscular status.
paper.rtp: The players were already fit and competing, so the study does not set return-to-sport criteria or show that these measures predict reinjury. It supports assessing movement strategy as well as jump outcome before full return, with eccentric force development as a possible rehabilitation focus, but it cannot be used to set a clearance threshold.
